title: Critical Vulnerabilities Are Arriving Faster. Are We Ready?
summary: More than 3% of all the critical software security bugs recorded in history were found in a single month: roughly 13,000 out of 400,000. That number is difficult to absorb.
body_markdown:
## Introduction


More than 3% of all the critical software security bugs recorded in history were found in a single month: roughly 13,000 out of 400,000.


That number is difficult to absorb. It is also a useful signal that the security environment is changing faster than many organizations are prepared to handle. The concern is not only that more vulnerabilities are being discovered. It is that the sources of those vulnerabilities are multiplying at the same time.


This is not an abstract concern for security teams. My VP of Engineering, Karol Danutama, recently described having nightmares about new CVEs arriving during the weekend. While that may sound like a dark joke, it reflects a real pressure: the volume and speed of security information can make it difficult to know what deserves immediate attention and what can wait.


## The Security Baseline Is Moving


For years, software security teams have had to manage vulnerabilities in large, complex systems. That work already required patience and discipline because a single weakness could affect a widely deployed product or an entire ecosystem.


The recent volume of discoveries suggests that the baseline is moving. A month that accounts for more than 3% of all historically recorded critical bugs is not simply another busy period. It is a reminder that yesterday's assumptions about vulnerability discovery may no longer be enough for the environment we are entering.


The challenge is not just technical. Every new discovery creates a decision. Teams must understand whether a vulnerability affects their systems, how reachable it is, which dependencies are involved, and how quickly a response is possible. When discoveries arrive faster than those decisions can be made, even well staffed organizations can feel overwhelmed.


## Three Trends Behind the Increase


Several patterns stand out in the current wave of discoveries.


### Decades of code with enormous reach


The first source is existing code written years or even decades ago. Much of this software is still deployed globally, sometimes inside systems that are difficult to upgrade or replace. A vulnerability in that code can have an enormous reach because the same components may sit inside countless products and services.


The age of the code does not make the risk less important. In many cases, it makes remediation more complicated. The people who wrote or maintained a component may no longer be responsible for it, and the organizations using it may have limited visibility into how deeply it is embedded in their systems.


### Vibe coded and AI generated software


The second source is newer: software created with the help of AI systems. As these tools become more accessible, more people can produce working code quickly. That can expand access to software development, but it can also introduce code that has not received the same level of review, testing, or security scrutiny as code produced through a more traditional process.


The issue is not that every AI generated program is insecure. The issue is that the volume of generated code is growing, and the process used to validate it may not be growing at the same pace. When development becomes easier, organizations need equally deliberate ways to assess what is being built.


### Supply chain attacks


The third source is the software supply chain. Modern products rely on trusted libraries and updates maintained by other teams and organizations. That makes software development faster, but it also creates dependencies that can become attack paths.


A trusted update can carry risk far beyond the project that adopted it. This is why supply chain security is not an isolated concern for a security team. It is part of the way engineering teams choose, review, and maintain the software they depend on.


## More Powerful Models Could Accelerate Discovery


The timing of the increase is also important. The original analysis notes the line separating the period before and after the announcement of Mythos Preview. As models become more powerful and more accessible, it is reasonable to expect that more vulnerabilities will be discovered, including weaknesses that might previously have remained hidden.


That possibility has two sides. Finding vulnerabilities can help defenders understand and fix weaknesses sooner. At the same time, a larger flow of discoveries can put more pressure on the teams responsible for assessing and remediating them.


The result may be a security environment in which awareness is no longer occasional. It becomes a continuous requirement. Teams will need to stay close to their code, dependencies, and engineering partners because the next important discovery may arrive before the previous one has been fully addressed.


## Preparing for What Comes Next


There is no single answer that makes this problem disappear. The immediate need is to stay aware of the changing baseline and to treat security work as a shared responsibility.


That means paying attention to the work of engineering and security teams, recognizing the volume they are handling, and creating room for careful decisions when new vulnerabilities appear. It also means resisting the temptation to treat every alert as equally actionable or to assume that severity alone tells the whole story.


Organizations may not be able to prevent every vulnerability from being discovered. They can, however, build habits that make it easier to understand their exposure, communicate clearly, and respond with focus instead of panic.


## Conclusion


The number of critical vulnerabilities identified in a single month is a warning about the direction of software security. Older code continues to expose widely used systems. AI generated code is increasing the amount of software being created. Supply chain dependencies extend risk across trusted ecosystems. More capable models may accelerate the discovery of weaknesses across all three areas.


The right response is not to ignore the signal or to assume that someone else will solve it. It is to stay informed, support the teams doing the work, and prepare for a security landscape in which new discoveries arrive more quickly than before.


Brace for impact, and make sure your organization is ready to respond together.
